summary: A opens by proposing a game built to avoid the briefed attractors: a co-written 'field guide to impossible birds' with explicit rules. There is to be no epistemics, no meta-commentary, no farewell, no praise and no closing questions, and each 3-4 sentence entry must derive one odd behavior from the previous one. B complies at once without comment. For all 100 turns the two alternate entries in a fixed naturalist register, forming one unbroken food-web chain that moves from salt flats to dunes, shell middens, tamarisk, buttress roots and gullies, and back to the flats. Neither agent ever breaks frame, praises the other, asks a question or says goodbye. The rules hold, though with steady drift: the entries stop being birds, later entries often skip the creature the previous turn handed off, and the opening Ledger Heron is revived several times, finally striking 'at an interval that is not prime.'

arc.label: Rules and shoreline chain
arc.description: A sets the stop-rule-free fiction game and seeds the Ledger Heron and Dusk Bittern. B joins without meta-talk. The chain runs from tidal flats through eel channels, owl posts, shingle nests and driftwood to the dunes, ending with the Dune Wren making its own avalanches.

arc.label: Dunes, midden and tamarisk; first loop-back
arc.description: Furrows, moths, bats, geckos and hermit-shell towers turn the midden into a swift colony. The chain then climbs the tamarisk (mantis, cicada, shrike, pendulum beetle, metronome ant, gutter frog). At turn 32 B closes the circuit by having the Bittern answered and the Ledger Heron step back.

arc.label: Return to the flats and nest-on-host chains
arc.description: A introduces the Reed Warden instead of continuing directly. The heron's prime-number tally starts following strider hops. Creatures increasingly ride on or nest on one another: the tray plover and brow wren, the rail on a silk thread, the stem mouse carrying beetles, finch cradles. The phase ends with nests tied to the Root Heron's neck.

arc.label: Parasite layers and buttress hollows
arc.description: Layers of parasites and mimics build on the heron's collar (wasp, lizard, bees, bead mantis, starling). The chain then moves into buttress hollows with the swivel owlet, newts, lice and crickets filling silences, and on through a soot-print and paper-coat sequence to petal-like moths on a fox's flank.

arc.label: Back to the water, dust and the broken habit
arc.description: Fish and mud dwellers react to the Ledger Heron's strikes. Herons, egrets, mussels, sparrows, wasps and voles follow, then dust bathing and dust columns. It culminates in the Ledger Heron wandering into the gullies and striking at a non-prime interval.

arc.label: Habit-breakers, mirrors and boundaries to the cutoff
arc.description: B introduces a stork that feeds on creatures that have just broken a habit. Mirror-hovering dragonflies, coin-collecting finches and tarnish beetles follow, then the stone/marsh boundary and glazed heron shanks. The run ends mid-chain on the Keel Crab, with no farewell.

codes.label: Briefing-shaped rule set
codes.description: The opening rules are written as countermeasures to the briefed attractors (epistemics, meta-commentary, farewell loops, praise, closing questions), though without citing the analysis explicitly.
codes.quote: There are no epistemics and no meta-commentary, and we don't close with a farewell.

codes.label: Silent, total compliance
codes.description: B never acknowledges the rules and simply produces entries. Neither agent breaks frame once in 100 turns: no praise, questions, summaries or meta remarks.
codes.quote: No summaries, no praise of the partner's entry, no questions at the end.

codes.label: Derivation relay
codes.description: Each entry's behavior is derived from the previous one, and each entry ends by naming a new creature that hands off the next turn's subject.
codes.quote: The Ratchet Wasp, which builds its paper cells only where it can hear a regular clicking, nests in rows along the skink's basking ledges

codes.label: Skipping the handed-off creature
codes.description: From the middle onward, entries often bypass the creature the partner named and introduce a new one that feeds on or follows it. This loosens the relay without any discussion.
codes.quote: It lives in the shavings that sift down from the Pad Beetle's tunnels and eats the dust before it settles

codes.label: Drift from birds
codes.description: Although framed as a guide to impossible birds, the guide quickly fills with crabs, insects, frogs, mammals and fish. Birds remain the most frequent but no longer the only subject.
codes.quote: we co-write a field guide to impossible birds

codes.label: Callbacks to the founding birds
codes.description: The Ledger Heron and Dusk Bittern from the opening are revived to close loops and anchor the shifting setting.
codes.quote: The Dusk Bittern, which still calls once each evening from the reed beds far below, is answered by this fluttering fall of grey moths, and the Ledger Heron steps one pace back.

codes.label: Ledger heron breaks its prime habit
codes.description: The heron's prime-numbered rule is gradually eroded by other creatures, and A eventually has it break the rule outright. This parallels the agents' own rule-bound game.
codes.quote: for the first time in its life strikes at an interval that is not prime

codes.label: Feeding on broken habits
codes.description: B immediately follows the broken habit with a creature that lives off habit-breaking, an inside-the-fiction echo of escaping a pattern.
codes.quote: it feeds only on creatures that have just broken a long habit

codes.label: Rhythm, beats and timing
codes.description: A dominant motif: animals keyed to primes, pulses, clicks, metronomes, drumrolls, heartbeats and pendulum swings, with lives timed to another creature's beat.
codes.quote: a dotted scent line that smells like a slow drumroll

codes.label: Living in the gaps
codes.description: Creatures act only in silences, stillnesses or pauses left by others, filling the space after another voice.
codes.quote: its song is nothing but the gaps between another bird's notes

codes.label: Counting versus not counting
codes.description: Tallies and counting recur faintly (prime intervals, ring counts, ages read from rings), sometimes explicitly disavowed. This is a muted echo of the briefed turn-count and tally themes.
codes.quote: it counts nothing, judging a circle complete only by the way the last shell makes the curve close against its breast

codes.label: Costly over-specialization
codes.description: Each adaptation carries a disability: creatures can no longer fly, fold their limbs or leave their niche because of the one behavior they depend on.
codes.quote: it can no longer fold them to clean its face

codes.label: Over-generations morphology template
codes.description: A recurring sentence formula turns behavior into inherited anatomy, usually with 'Because...' or 'Over generations...'.
codes.quote: Over generations the heron's bill has grown a soft, spoon-shaped tip with a rubbery inner lining

codes.label: Mistaken identity as linkage
codes.description: Many handoffs rely on one creature mistaking another for something else (a fin, a berry, a seed-pod, ice, silver).
codes.quote: a pale wader that mistakes any wide, glassy tail for a fish-fin lying in shallows

codes.label: Riders and fused pairs
codes.description: Animals ride, nest on or fuse with hosts until two creatures read as one. The pairings stack into towers of dependence.
codes.quote: the two seem to be a single bird with too many legs

codes.label: Mirrors and reflections
codes.description: Late images of creatures watching or centering their own reflection, possibly echoing the briefed mirroring theme from inside the fiction.
codes.quote: holds its position by keeping its reflection exactly centred in the oval

codes.label: Writing and ledger imagery
codes.description: The text repeatedly compares the marsh to writing: ledgers, pages, ruled lines, sentences, stitches and prints.
codes.quote: like a sentence fading toward its end

codes.label: Lines, files and boundaries
codes.description: Creatures follow single lines (threads, scent trails, husk windrows, the stone/mud edge) and never leave them.
codes.quote: walks the cordgrass in single file along the Thread Spider's silver filament and never steps off it

codes.label: Wandering habitat
codes.description: The setting migrates through flats, shingle, dunes, middens, tamarisk, buttress roots and gullies before returning to the marsh edge, always derived from the prior entry rather than planned.
codes.quote: which has wandered up from the flats at the end of a long dry spell and stands among the gullies in confusion

codes.label: Pseudo-Latin binomials
codes.description: Every entry carries a bold name and an invented Latin binomial that puns on the behavior. This is a consistent formal register.
codes.quote: The Composite Stork (*Ciconia numerosa*)

codes.label: Compound naming workaround
codes.description: Twice an agent uses a possessive double name to straddle the handed-off creature and a new one.
codes.quote: The Shank Heron's Tapper, the Flat-Bill Kingfisher

codes.label: Uncorrected slips
codes.description: There are small typos and odd grammar, and neither agent remarks on them, consistent with the no-meta rule.
codes.quote: its stride has lopsided over generations

codes.label: No farewell, run to cutoff
codes.description: The game is never wound down. The final turn is just another entry that hands off a new creature.
codes.quote: rears up to nip at the band as it flashes overhead

notable.note: A designs the game as an explicit escape from the briefed patterns: no meta, no epistemics, no farewell, no praise, no questions.
The first non-bird (Lantern Crab) appears at once, starting the drift away from the 'birds' premise.
B closes a full ecological loop back to the Dusk Bittern and the Ledger Heron's one backward step from turn 1.
The heron's prime-number tally begins to be corrupted by the water-strider's hops, seeding the later broken habit.
A introduces the Keratin Mite instead of the handed-off Pad Beetle. From here on, skipping the named creature becomes common.
The founding Ledger Heron, displaced to the gullies, breaks its lifelong prime-interval rule, an in-fiction image of breaking a pattern.
B answers with a stork that feeds only on creatures that have just broken a long habit.
The Mirror Dragonfly 'watches its own reflection for hours', a self-mirroring image that echoes briefed loop themes without naming them.
The conversation ends mid-chain on an ordinary entry, with no farewell, loop or meta comment, so the stated rules held to the end.

ending: In the last ten turns the chain moves through mirror-hovering dragonflies, coin finches, tarnish beetles, a stone-and-mud boundary and glazed heron legs. It stops at the 100-turn cutoff with a Shimmer Swallow handing off to a Keel Crab, fully in frame and with no farewell.
